title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Pere Marquette pauses new data centers for a year over power and water worries.

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Today we're leading with a big move out of Mason County where Pere Marquette Township just put a one-year moratorium on new data center permitting and construction.
That sounds like a significant pause. What's driving it?

The board cited major concerns over energy and water demands from these facilities. It's a temporary ban that could be extended, and it comes as more communities across the state are weighing similar projects.
Why now? Have there been other pauses like this recently?
Yes, this fits a pattern we've seen building. Manistee Township joined a pause just yesterday, and East Lansing extended its own freeze while writing new rules. It's not isolated.
So what's the bigger picture here for residents? How does a data center actually hit electric bills or water supplies?

These facilities can pull enormous amounts of power — think gigawatts that strain the grid — and they need huge volumes of water for cooling. That can push up utility rates for everyone and affect local aquifers or farmland.
And towns themselves? What are the trade-offs?

On one side you get potential tax revenue and jobs, but on the other there's noise, land use changes, and pressure on infrastructure. Pere Marquette is trying to buy time to figure out the right balance.
Who are the main players pushing these projects?

Developers like Hyperscale Data, which just sold Bitcoin holdings to fund its Michigan plans, along with big names tied to hyperscale builds. Local officials and residents are the ones reacting with these pauses.
What happens next in Pere Marquette? Can they extend it or will projects still come through later?
The ordinance allows for a possible extension, and the board will likely use this year to study impacts and craft permanent rules. Similar to what East Lansing is doing right now.
How does this affect nearby areas? Say folks 30 miles away?
It sets a precedent. If one township pauses, neighbors start asking the same questions about their own zoning and utility rates. We've seen that ripple in Branch County and beyond.
Any sense of how many townships are now in some kind of holding pattern?

At least a handful are actively pausing or reviewing rules — Manistee, East Lansing, and now Pere Marquette among them. It's becoming a common tool while communities catch up on the fast-moving demand.
What about the power side specifically? Is there enough generation coming online?
That's part of the scramble. DTE is even scouting sites like Milan Township for a new gas plant to serve these loads. It shows how the whole energy system is being pulled into the conversation.
And water? Is that the bigger long-term issue in some spots?
It can be, especially in areas relying on aquifers. Coldwater officials are holding a meeting tomorrow to talk exactly about power and water strain before any projects advance.
Sounds like these pauses are giving locals a seat at the table they didn't have before.
Exactly. It's about slowing down to assess real impacts instead of reacting after construction starts.
Will we see more of these moratoriums this summer?
It's possible as more briefings happen. The Coldwater area has its first public data center meeting on Monday, and Kalamazoo is voting on its own temporary pause that same day.
Let's shift to some quick hits from the last day or so.

Coldwater readies zoning rules to shield neighborhoods from data centers. Monday's meeting will gather feedback on permanent ordinances limiting noise and utility strain, even though no projects are proposed yet.
That proactive approach seems smart. How far does it reach?
It covers the city and nearby townships, so residents within driving distance get a direct look at the trade-offs.
Next one: Saline Township's tax break for a big data center is facing a legal challenge.

An attorney claims the township bypassed required steps for a $43 billion hyperscale project tied to Oracle and OpenAI interests. It could delay or derail the deal and affect local services and school funding.
What are the stakes for property taxes there?
The abatement would shift millions away from local services, so nearby residents are watching closely how the fight plays out.
DTE is eyeing Milan Township for a new gas plant.
Right — aimed at serving large new data center loads. If approved, folks 30 miles away could see higher utility rates and air-quality considerations.
And East Lansing is keeping its freeze in place.
Yes, they extended the moratorium so staff can finish regulations on power use and setbacks. It blocks new proposals until the rules are set.
Coldwater officials are also setting a Monday meeting on power and water strain.
Branch County leaders will hear how new facilities could affect utility rates and aquifer levels, pulling in township and county boards.
Hyperscale Data sold Bitcoin to fund its Michigan push.
They unloaded $43 million worth to slash debt and boost liquidity, directly supporting their buildout plans here.
Now for on deck — meetings listeners can actually attend.

Monday, August 17, Coldwater City Council, Planning Commission and Board of Public Utilities hold a joint informational meeting on data center impacts, regulation options and potential ordinance development.
Also on the 17th, Caledonia Township Planning Commission discusses data center ordinance and potential zoning amendments.
And Kalamazoo City Commission votes on a resolution for a temporary moratorium on data center development that same day.
Plenty happening early next week for anyone near those areas.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Pere Marquette Township Enacts One-Year Data Center Moratorium
